title: Awakening

teacherSummary.text: Walking away, Siddhartha realizes he has always fled from himself and resolves to learn from himself. Suddenly the world appears new and beautiful—colors, rivers, forests—no longer illusion but reality to be experienced. He feels a chill of loneliness: he is no longer a Brahmin or a Samana, but he will not go home.

vocabulary.context: I searched Atman, I searched Brahman, I was willing to dissect my self and peel off all of its layers, to find the core of all peels in its unknown interior, the Atman, life, the divine part, the ultimate part.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dissect”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To breathe or draw into the lungs
vocabulary.context: Deeply, he inhaled, and for a moment, he felt cold and shivered.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act of deceiving or misleading
vocabulary.context: “When someone reads a text, wants to discover its meaning, he will not scorn the symbols and letters and call them deceptions, coincidence, and worthless hull, but he will read them, he will study and love them, letter by letter.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deception”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act or state of one who, or that which, heads
vocabulary.context: And it was not long until he walked again in long strides, started to proceed swiftly and impatiently, heading no longer for home, no longer to his father, no longer back.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “heading”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act or business of instructing
vocabulary.context: He had also left the last teacher who had appeared on his path, even him, the highest and wisest teacher, the most holy one, Buddha, he had left him, had to part with him, was not able to accept his teachings.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To walk with long steps, especially in a measured or pompous manner
vocabulary.context: And it was not long until he walked again in long strides, started to proceed swiftly and impatiently, heading no longer for home, no longer to his father, no longer back.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “stride”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: One who, or that which, works
vocabulary.context: There was no nobleman who did not belong to the noblemen, no worker that did not belong to the workers, and found refuge with them, shared their life, spoke their language.

context.history: In Hindu thought, Maya is the veil of illusion over the world; Siddhartha turns away from seeing the world as Maya.

significance: This epiphany marks the end of Part One and turns him toward sensory life.
discussionQuestions: What changes in how Siddhartha sees the world in this chapter?

How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the river and time?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Awakening,” how does Hesse show awakening to the world? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Awakening develops the idea of awakening to the world. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses imagery in Awakening to complicate the reader's understanding of awakening to the world. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Awakening within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of awakening to the world responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Awakening as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of awakening to the world. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

options: A visible sign or representation of an idea

satQuestions.passage: When Siddhartha left the grove, where the Buddha, the perfected one, stayed behind, where Govinda stayed behind, then he felt that in this grove his past life also stayed behind and parted from him. He pondered about this sensation, which filled him completely, as he was slowly walking along. He pondered deeply, like diving into a deep water he let himself sink down to the ground of the sensation, down to the place where the causes lie, because to identify the causes, so it seemed to him, is the very essence of thinking, and by this alone sensations turn into realizations and are not lost, but become entities and start to emit like rays of light what is inside of them.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Awakening”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What changes in how Siddhartha sees the world in this chapter? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are dissect, inhaled, deceptions, heading, teachings. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I searched Atman, I searched Brahman, I was willing to dissect my self and peel off all of its layers, to find the core of all peels in its unknown interior, the Atman, life, the divine part, the ultimate part.” Webster's says: (Anat.) To divide into separate parts. Now the word history: “dissect”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “inhale”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “deception”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. In Hindu thought, Maya is the veil of illusion over the world; Siddhartha turns away from seeing the world as Maya. Why does this chapter matter? This epiphany marks the end of Part One and turns him toward sensory life. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for imagery.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see imagery, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to awakening to the world.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Imagery, Symbolism, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of imagery. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

He pondered deeply, like diving into a deep water he let himself sink down to the ground of the sensation, down to the place where the causes lie, because to identify the causes, so it seemed to him, is the very essence of thinking, and by this alone sensations turn into realizations and are not lost, but become entities and start to emit like rays of light what is inside of them.

Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence. segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
